input.short_description: Load historical data into your pipeline and backfill your destination with past events.
input.body:
Backfill historical data

This recipe shows you how to load historical data into your pipeline and populate your destination with events from the past.

Overview

Backfilling is useful when you're setting up a new pipeline but need to ensure your destination has all historical data, not just future events from the moment the pipeline goes live.

Steps

1. Prepare your historical data source

Export your historical data in a format compatible with Godzilla (JSON lines, CSV, or your connector's native format). Ensure the data includes the same fields your live pipeline will receive.

2. Create or configure a batch source connector

Set up a source connector that can read your historical dataset in bulk. This might be a file-based connector, database query, or API paginator.

3. Run the backfill pipeline

Create a separate pipeline or trigger your existing pipeline with the historical data source. Monitor the pipeline to ensure all records are processed without errors.

4. Verify completeness

Once the backfill completes, compare record counts and spot-check samples in your destination to confirm all historical data was transferred.

5. Switch to the live source

Once backfilling is complete and verified, update your pipeline to use the live data source for ongoing ingestion.

Best practices

  • Run backfills during off-peak hours to minimize impact on live traffic.
  • Use idempotent transformations so backfill data can be re-ingested safely if needed.
  • Enable comprehensive logging during backfill to troubleshoot any failures.
  • Keep a record of what data was backfilled and when for audit purposes.

input.short_description: Route a single pipeline's output to multiple destinations with conditional logic.
input.body:
Fan-out to multiple destinations

This recipe shows you how to take events from a single source and route them to multiple destination systems based on conditions or event properties.

Overview

Fan-out (or fanout) is a common pattern where a single data stream is split and sent to multiple endpoints. This is useful for replicating data across systems, A/B testing, or sending different event types to specialized handlers.

Steps

1. Create a source connector

Set up your source connector to ingest events. This will feed into a transform layer that makes routing decisions.

2. Add conditional transform logic

In your pipeline's transform step, evaluate event properties and attach metadata that indicates which destination(s) the event should reach. For example, tag events based on event type, customer tier, or content category.

3. Create multiple destination connectors

Configure separate destination connectors for each target system. You may have one for a data warehouse, one for a real-time analytics platform, and another for an operational database.

4. Route based on tags or conditions

In a final transform step or via destination-specific filters, use the tags or conditions you added in step 2 to control which events flow to each destination.

5. Monitor and adjust

Watch event flow to each destination to ensure routing is correct. Adjust filter conditions as business requirements evolve.

Best practices

  • Use consistent naming for tags or routing fields across all events.
  • Log routing decisions at transform time for debugging and auditing.
  • Test your conditional logic with sample events before processing production data.
  • Monitor throughput and latency separately for each destination to catch bottlenecks.
  • Consider using a message broker or queue if you need temporal decoupling between split and delivery.
